chapters.title: Scene 1 - Duplicator
chapters.content:
It was late afternoon, sometime in my third year of elementary school,
the sun already slanting toward the hills.
I went to the schoolyard with my older sister
and a few of her friends, just to pass the time.


Near the sink, beside the art room,
our homeroom teacher was pulling open a large drawer.

From inside emerged, one by one:
a dark blue ink container,
a rubber roller,
and a square wooden frame.


The class president stood next to him,
and the air carried the unmistakable feeling
that something important was about to happen.


We couldn't contain our curiosity
and ran straight over.

"Teacher, what are you doing?"

"I'm printing the test papers.

Wanna help?"


Before he even finished the sentence,
we shouted back in unison,

"Yes~~!"



The teacher stretched the paraffin sheet tight
across the mimeograph frame—
a thing that looked like a construction-site sand sieve.


My older sister rolled the ink onto the board,
feeding the rubber roller until it shone dark and wet.
I carefully slid the thin test paper
under the frame, one sheet at a time.


Then the teacher pushed the roller—
shhk—


and on the rough, gray paper,
crooked, pale letters slowly appeared.


The smell of ink stabbed my nose,
but I didn't mind it at all.
Inside that smell was the feeling
that we were doing something important.


We printed sixty sheets.
Not a single one of us complained.



Printing the test papers took only a moment,
but writing the questions for them
took days.


The teacher would place the paraffin sheet
on a metal plate
and, with a pen that released no ink,
carve each question line by line into the surface.


Watching that, I thought to myself,
There's no way I could ever be a schoolteacher...
I already hated dictation as it was.


When test day came,
cries erupted from every corner of the classroom.

"Teacher, I can't read it!"

During math especially,

2 and 3, 8 and 9
were impossible to tell apart,
and the confusion only grew.

We did look at the test questions—

at least, technically we did—
but there was no way to tell what we were looking at.
The quality of those test papers was so miserable
that most of the time the teacher ended up
rewriting every question on the blackboard
before we could even start the exam.

Under those conditions,

cheating wasn't even a concept.
There was nothing clear enough to cheat from.

One day, while I was playing with Minji—

my desk partner from the neighborhood—
I told her about helping print the test papers.
When she heard that we had another test the next day,
she panicked and insisted we come up with a countermeasure.
Thus began our grand conspiracy:
the test paper leak.


Plan 1:
Help with the mimeograph printing
and secretly memorize the questions.


Plan 2:
If the printing was already finished,
they must have thrown the scrap sheets away—
so we'd dig through the trash
and recover the test papers.



We marched to school full of grand ambition—
only to find that the mimeograph work was already finished,
and the trash cans had been cleaned out spotless.

Minji collapsed in despair.

"How am I supposed to take the test tomorrow?
I can't study at all..."

So I said, casually,

"I'll let you copy mine tomorrow."

Her eyes lit up instantly.
"If I do well on the test,
I'll give you all my marbles—every single one!
So you gotta show me properly, okay?"

The next day during class,

our homeroom teacher handed back the graded tests.

I got a hundred.

She got ninety.

I leaned over and whispered to Minji,

"You know you gotta give me all your marbles later, right?"
I said it with a straight face.

She stayed quiet until the very end of class.

Then, the moment recess—play time—started,
she bolted out of the classroom.

I ran after her,

but she kept sprinting
until she dove into the girls' restroom
and locked the door from the inside.

I picked up a small stone

and wedged it under the door from the outside
so it couldn't be pushed open.
Then I calmly went back to the classroom.


But Minji—who I thought would come out soon—

never returned, even after the next class began.

Suddenly, fear hit me.

All kinds of thoughts ran through my head,
and then one horrible idea flashed up:
What if she slipped and drowned in the toilet?

A chill ran through my whole body.

I told the teacher I needed to go to the bathroom,

then hurried back to the restroom
where I had wedged the stone under the door.

From inside,

I heard Minji crying.

Every time she pushed the door outward,

the stone stayed jammed tight
between the door and the floor,
refusing to budge.

"Minji, move away from the door!" I shouted,

then kicked it hard from the outside—bang, bang.

The stone popped loose and rolled away,

and Minji stumbled out,
her face a mess of tears and snot.

"Are you okay?" I asked.

She didn't answer.

She just kept crying
and walked straight back to the classroom.

After that, Minji never spoke to me again.

I was just relieved that Minji was safe.
After that, I made up my mind never to fool around in a bathroom again.


And on my elementary school report card,
there was always the same line written every year:


"Plays pranks excessively."

chapters.title: Scene 2 - Food Poisoning
chapters.content:
According to my mother, once my father made up his mind to close down the boarding house, there were all sorts of dealings back and forth for days. In the end, he handed the place over to one of his old friends.

Whenever my father was out of sight, I used to wander over to Jungho's house.

The moment you opened their door, you could smell the way that family lived. Beside the gate stood a strange bonsai—branches twisted like snakes climbing a tree. At the end of the wooden porch sat a tiny apple tree, bearing red fruits no bigger than a marble, shining brrrrightly, pretty as lacquer.

But if you plucked one and bit into it, your mouth went dry as dust and you'd spit it out.

"Tweh! Tweh-tweh!"

Then the adults behind you would burst out laughing.

"It's only pretty to look at, kid."

In the old guest room, Father and his friends used to kill time with mahjong or cards. They would stack mahjong tiles like a wall, rattle the dice, line up those thin white sticks, and play with loud thunk, thunk sounds.

I didn't know a single rule, but I'd crouch behind Father, watch that secret world of grown-ups, and eventually doze off right there.

One evening, Mother called Seonju-nuna in a hurry.

"Hey, come with me—quick."

And they left for Jungho's house.

Two hours later, Mother slammed the door as she came in and clicked her tongue.

"Aigo... people say raising sons is useless. Damn it! Idiots!"

I was digging my ear and asked,

"What happened?"

Seonju-nuna let out a long sigh.

"Jungho's mom got food poisoning. She threw up and had diarrhea... ruined all her clothes and blankets."

I snorted.

"That's nothing. Just wash it."

Nuna shook her head.

"That's not the problem. She stayed like that for two whole days because the men in the house didn't change her clothes."

My eyes grew round.

"What? Why not?"

"They were supposed to wash her, but they... couldn't bring themselves to pull down their own mother's underclothes. When she asked why, they said, 'How can we undress our mother down there?' and froze."

I let out a helpless laugh.

"Well... that house is full of men. That must've been rough."

But Nuna kept looking straight at me.

"Then tell me, if our mother ends up like that someday, what will you do?"

I scratched my head.

"Who knows? Probably all the aunties will come running. Chungju-aunt, Jeongchachon-sister-in-law..."

"What if nobody's around?"

Nuna's voice was serious.

I paused.

"You mean—just sons at home? Then our mother will handle it herself. She's got the temper of a tiger. Even twenty grown men together can't stop her."

Nuna giggled.

"True. Even smallpox and tiger ghosts would step aside for Mother."

I dug my ear again.

"I'll ask Father-in-law tomorrow. If you ever get food poisoning... I guess I'll be the one to clean it, right?"

Nuna's face suddenly flushed red. She bit her lip.

"We still didn't have any... honey~~~"

She tried to continue, but pinched her thigh to keep from laughing.

I pretended not to notice.

"What? Honey? Pot? Party? You speak English loud today? Then why are you pinching that poor little thigh?"

Nuna jumped back, flustered.

"I—I suddenly have stomachache!"

And she ran out of the room like she was escaping a crime scene.

Watching her flee, I scratched my nose and murmured,

"Life's got no answers... when even mothers and sons turn out like this."

chapters.title: Scene 3 - Letter from Odin's Kingdom 2
chapters.content:
Dearest! Mein Kaiser!

You once told me that a tree cannot simply be transplanted into foreign soil. Only now do I understand the full weight of that truth.

Here in Odin's Kingdom, ghosts live completely severed from their own realm.

No safety nets.
No redemption arcs.
No "next life."

Just taxes, survival, and the cold wind that polishes the bone.

But in your kingdom?

A ghost may sin, be punished, serve the sentence, and rise again—
not as ash, but as life.

Your welfare system... yes, it empties my pockets—
but at least it exists.

Here?

Only frost.

Humans distrust ghosts, ghosts distrust humans, and neither side bothers to listen to the other's heartbeat.

And yet—
I have made a friend.

Her name is Huldra.

We grew close sharing the kimchi and ramyeon you sent. She called the taste "heaven-warm"—a warmth she had never touched in life or in death.

If you ever open a gate in your kingdom, she wishes to follow me through it.

Sincerely,
your loyal trainee.


P.S.

"General, your kingdom is strange.
In your land, even ghosts are given a second life.
Here in Odin's world, we don't get 'second.'
We barely get 'first.'"

"In your land, a ghost who makes a mistake goes to prison, yes—
but afterward they are allowed to be reborn,
to work again,
to love again.
That is mercy.
That is welfare.
That is dignity."

"But here?
We pay our tax,
we starve alone,
we freeze alone,
and no human hears our voices.
Your kingdom feels... warmer than life itself."

"General, I finally understand what you meant:
Even the dead deserve a chance to live."

chapters.title: Scene 4 - Dandelion Pickle
chapters.content:
I was in second grade, so most of it has faded, but I still remember this much:

On the way down to the wash place, my mother set big and small stones into the mud, pressing them down with her bare hands to make steps for the women to walk safely.

That path led to a wide field—forty meters across, maybe two hundred meters long. Its edges were walled with earth and stone, a meter high, like a small fortress. Hard to reach unless you knew where to climb.

When winter loosened its grip, when the ice cracked and the willow buds fluffed out—the village women headed to that field with baskets on their heads and children dangling from their hands.

I wasn't supposed to run around like other kids. I took medicine every day, and my body was always a little slower, a little weaker. But the older girls never went without me.

They'd break off willow buds and press them into my palms.

Soft as rabbit fur.
Warm as a quilt straight from sunlight.

While the children chased each other in the grass, the women knelt with their hoes, digging up 'Naeng-i' and 'mugwort'. The older girls helped—cheeks flushed, sleeves rolled, like they were already small versions of the women they would someday become.

After an hour or two, when the baskets were half full of spring greens, the girls finally sat in a circle and began making dandelion jewelry.

Seon-ae-nuna—golden-handed Seon-ae—and Kongju-nuna braided crowns, rings, and necklaces. Their hair caught the spring light, and the crowns glowed like halos.

Of course I begged for one. So they made me a tiny crown too.

The dandelion stems—thin, bright, green with a hint of blue—looked fragile, but once woven, they held together like rope.

We wore our crowns, rings on our fingers, and chased each other across the field until the sky began to cool.

The next morning, our house filled with the smell of 'Naengi Doenjang Soup'—spring in a bowl.

The day after that, the women mixed mugwort into dough and made 'Sugbeomuri'—a kind of mugwort rice cake to share with every house.

But my mother—she saved the dandelion stems. She washed them clean, tied them in bundles, and placed them into an earthen jar.

Then she boiled soy sauce and poured it over them—'Dandelion Jang-a-jji'.

A month later, we ate it with dalrae namul.

Salty, bitter, sweet.
Like the taste of early spring.

But those spring days didn't last.

Maybe I was in fourth grade when the typhoon came. Rain hammered the ground for days. The adults couldn't sleep—worried the river would overflow.

We children peeked outside, just to see how high the water was rising. Even that was enough to be scolded.

"It's dangerous! Back inside—NOW!"

The water kept climbing, brown and heavy, like a beast waking up.

On TV they said pigs from farmhouses were being swept away. I stared at the river and felt something cold in my bones.

In the end, the river didn't flood the village—but it did take everything else.

The field where we ran.
The earthen wall like a fortress.
The small plots above it.

Gone.
All gone.

The ground looked as if a 'Gigantic Cat' had dragged its claws through it—a long, quiet wound left on the land.

Later, the county rebuilt the land with retaining walls and concrete channels. But the place where we laughed, the place where spring lived—that never came back.

That was the year I learned nature isn't "pretty." It's an emperor. It gives, and it takes, without apology.

chapters.title: Scene 5 - Bossam-jil (Widow-napping)
chapters.content:
There was one rule in our house that could never be broken.

"Save on anything you want—
but never on books."

So my mother bought the entire 500-volume set
of the Ministry of Education's Recommended Books for Youth
and lined one side of our living room wall
with a heavy, imposing bookshelf.

Every month she subscribed to Newton,
and never missed an issue of Sonyeon Joongang or Bomulseom.
The stories poured into our home
like mischievous children
who never knew how to behave.

I remember thinking,
There's no way I'll ever read all of this.

But that's how life works.
In the end,
I read almost all of it.

In Eunpunggol,
big and small troubles
always seemed to pass through our house first.

One summer,
a man from the village ran off
with a widow.
It was a clumsy kind of bossam-jil.

Her father was furious,
and the man had nothing—
no money,
no place to hide.

In the end,
he brought the widow
straight to our house,
threw himself down on the wooden porch,
and begged my mother to save them.

My mother seated the two of them on the porch.
She didn't raise her voice.
She didn't get angry.

After a long silence,
she spoke.

"Juguk," she said.
"This isn't something
that can be brushed aside."

Then she added,

"You may have to lose a finger."

At those words,
Juguk and Yeon-hui
said nothing.

That very night,
the two of them fled the village.

A few days later,
people said,

"If they don't even have that kind of nerve,
raising children would be impossible anyway."

And that was the end of it.

That night,
I told the story to Seonju.

She stayed silent for a long time.

I spoke quietly.

"Getting married,
having children—
those aren't things you start
without thinking."

After a brief pause,
I added,

"It's something you enter
with your life on the line."


Seonju smiled and asked,

"So... did you risk your life
to marry me too?"

I pointed to the bookshelf.

"Pick a book."

She pulled out Samgang Oryun
and So-nyeo-gyeong.

"I know this one," she said,
"but what on earth
is this shameless book?"

"That shameless book," I replied,
"was officially designated
as recommended reading for teenagers
by the Ministry of Education."

"For real?"

"Want me to call my mom?"

"No!
I'm just... trying to understand."

"I don't teach for free.
What are you going to give me?"

"What do I even have to give?"

"Then at least act cute.
My mother always said—
a man can live with a clever fox,
but never with a clueless bear."

After hesitating for a long moment,
Seonju twisted her body awkwardly and said,

"Honeyyy~~
my sweet honeyyy~~
this foolish maiden wishes to learn.
Won't you teach me~?"

That night,
I gave her a small lecture.

"Samgang Oryun
is a moral code from the Joseon era.
Even now, during holidays or ancestral rites,
you still hear elders quote it.

But modern scholars don't think
it fits our time anymore.
Sex education is necessary, of course,
but teaching it openly
always causes trouble.

So they slipped it quietly
into the list of recommended books,
hoping kids would figure things out on their own.

Maybe that was
the last bit of conscience
our intellectuals had left."

"Juguk's case was the same.
They had to be shamed in front of the village elders—
that was the only way
they could stand upright afterward.

Normally,
a man confesses his feelings,
the woman accepts,
they greet the elders,
and then the families exchange a proper proposal.

There's an order to these things.

If you skip all that
and jump straight to bossam?
That's not romance.
That's kidnapping.

Even back in the Joseon era,
there were unspoken ways
to tell whether two people
were truly in love."

Seonju stared at me.

"And how do you know all this,
my dear husband?"

"Read a 500-volume collection cover to cover
and live with my mother for ten years.
After that,
you just know things automatically."

She opened So-nyeo-gyeong,
her eyes narrowing.

"Then...
how do you do this part?"

"That," I said,
"requires a monthly tuition fee."

She pouted and spread out the blanket.

"This poor maiden
has no such fee..."

"I told you earlier—
a woman must be a fox,
not a bear."

Suddenly she jumped up and started dancing.

"You are the dancing queen~
young and sweet~~~~"

The rafters shook.
The brass pots in the kitchen rattled.
Even the jars in the yard
seemed to dance along.

That night,
Madam Chungju leaned toward my mother
and whispered,

"Those two...
they're going to break every honeypot
in this house tonight."

My mother didn't even blink.
She simply nodded and murmured,

"It's their season now... isn't it?"

chapters.title: Scene 6 - Guest from Odin's Kingdom
chapters.content:
Ms. M returned from Odin's Kingdom.
She bowed deeply before Yeomra, the King of Death,
and then came straight to me—
someone quiet, tall, and unfamiliar walking behind her.

Ms. M
"General! Please allow me to bow to you first!"

I laughed softly.
"Well, well... the King already told me everything."

Ms. M
"Thanks to you, I learned so much.
I experienced things I never imagined.
From now on, I will serve you with all my loyal heart."

Me
"Graduated cum laude, huh? I'm proud of you.
You're no longer just a ghost or a messenger—you know that, right?"


Ms. M
"Yes, sir! Ready for orders, sir!"

Me
"Easy. You need a proper rest.
With your family... and with your new husband.
But before that—I hear you brought me a guest."

Ms. M
"Yes, sir. This is Huldra, from Odin's Kingdom.
Huldra, please introduce yourself to my General."

Huldra bowed so gracefully it almost looked like a ritual.

Huldra
"General... I humbly present myself.
It is an honor to meet you.
My king—Odin—often spoke of you.
He said, 'Nothing in this world or the next can compare to him.'"

Me
"I used to visit Odin's Kingdom for chess.
He was one of my toughest opponents.
Huldra—from today on, you follow my rules.
Agent M, guide her to her new quarters."

Huldra
"Thank you, sir!"

I added, almost as an afterthought—

Me
"And... about that incident.
You have my thanks.
You saved a girl—Nadia Comăneci.

Some fool down here fell in love with her just from watching TV.

And worse—even a Dokkaebi became obsessed.
If you hadn't intervened,
we would've had chaos... on both sides."

Agent M
"...Sir, the Dokkaebi kept shouting,
'How can a human bend like that?! She must be one of us!!'
It took three officers to hold him down."

I groaned.

Me
"That creature always falls for the wrong women.
First Vanna White...
Then Nadia Comăneci...
What's next? Princess Diana?"

Huldra whispered, puzzled—

Huldra
"...What is a TV?"

Me
"You'll find one in your room.
Go see it yourself. But don't fall in love with anyone."

I waved my hand.

"Alright—meetingdismissed. Go home. Rest."

chapters.title: Scene 7 - Taste of Tobacco
chapters.content:
There was a small tobacco shop right next to our house.
Sirak lived there with his grandmother,
and I ran errands for them almost every day—
buying cigarettes with names that sounded like magic spells.

Hwanhee, Sol, 88, Hansando, Taeyang, Saemaeul, Rose...

My father usually smoked Hwanhee or Sol,
and my mother preferred 88.
Even now, I can't explain why that number—88—
looked so cool and confident on a cigarette pack.
Back then, those brand names felt like tiny passwords
to a world only adults were allowed to ente

Between Sirak's tobacco shop and the hardware store next door
ran a narrow alley—
just wide enough for kids to squeeze in sideways
and just secret enough to feel like our own kingdom.

That was where Sirak and the neighborhood boys gathered every day,
playing marbles, slapping down paper game cards,
spinning tops until the dirt floor trembled.

Sirak was always inventing a new game,
a new rule,
a new kind of mischief.

To us,
he wasn't just the oldest kid in the alley—
he was the undisputed boss of our little world.

One early winter day,
Sirak-hyung was hammering and scraping away at something—
ttuk-ttak, sseuk-sseuk-ssak-ssak—
so I went to see what he was up to.

It was a sled.

The other boys quickly copied him,
but I was clumsy and kept fumbling with the wood.
Sirak-hyung watched me struggle for a moment,
then built one for me in just a few strokes—
clean, swift, effortless.

Sirak's family also farmed tobacco.
In summer, they harvested the long, heavy leaves,
steamed them in a great curing barn,
dried them until they turned the color of old brass,
and sold them to the Korea Tobacco & Ginseng Corporation.


One afternoon after school,
I stopped by Sirak-hyung's place.
His family—and half the neighborhood kids—
were threading tobacco leaves onto long ropes,
one leaf after another,

like stringing beads of sunlight.

We thought it was the funniest thing,
so we giggled and helped,
our small hands clumsy but eager,
laughing at how the leaves brushed our faces
with their sweet, earthy smell.

Then one of the elders said,
"If you dry these right and smoke them in a 'Gom-bang-dae' pipe,
the flavor is unbelievable."

One kid piped up with a snort,
"But I heard the ones you buy at the store taste better than that!"

The elder clicked his tongue.
"Aish—what do you kids know about the taste of tobacco?"

"Maybe it tastes bad 'cause you messed it up.
Simple as that~."

The adults burst into loud laughter.
"Our Dong-gi really knows a thing or two!
Alright then—can you teach us how to make tobacco taste good?"

I nodded like a little master.
"Well, it depends on what each gentleman likes.
...some elders like it sweet—add a little sugar and a pinch of MSG, you know, that seasoning powder called Miwon."
And some of you like it sharp and cool—so you mix in peppermint or a touch of cinnamon."


The adults roared with laughter,
slapping their knees and wiping their eyes.

Then one mischievous elder leaned in and asked
"Well then, how do you make it... nutty?"

I suddenly realized,
"Ah... this is grown-ups teasing me."

So I thought of that nutty sesame-oil smell
that rises when you roll gimbap—
and a brilliant idea struck me:

"If you brush sesame oil on tobacco leaves
and then smoke them...
wouldn't they smell wonderfully nutty too?"

So I answered with complete seriousness.

"Oh, that one's a bit tricky," I replied gravely.
"First, you dry the leaves perfectly and press them flat.
Then you brush them—very gently—with sesame oil,
let them rest in the shade for a week,
sprinkle just a pinch of seasoned salt,
and finally grill them over charcoal...
front and back... just a little... just enough."

By this point, the adults were laughing so hard
they were wiping tears from their eyes.

"Our Dong-gi knows every tobacco flavor!"
one of them hollered.
"Look at him—he's the greatest elder in all of Eunpunggol!"

And before I knew what was happening,
they hoisted me up onto someone's shoulders,
parading me around the alley
like I'd just become the village chief.

Seeing all this, the other elders turned to my mother and said:

"Where on earth did you get a boy like that?"
"Unbelievable—absolutely unexplainable how sharp he is."
"That kid's silver tongue is the best in the whole village!"
"I swear, Eunpunggol might finally have a true prodigy."

My mother listened to their praise
with a quiet, satisfied smile.

That night, Seonju spoke up.
"Seobangnim-Honey... will you teach me how cigarettes taste?"

I snapped back, playing the stern husband,
"Hey now—kids shouldn't know such things."


She burst into laughter,
and the sound of it—light, careless, warm—
slipped out the window
and drifted into the alley where summer was ending.

And just like that,
between the fading heat of August
and the first chilly breath of autumn,
the two of us were tangled
in a season of sweet, ridiculous days.

chapters.title: Scene 8 - A man from GIA (Ghost Intelligence Agency)
chapters.content:
A man from GIA(Ghost Intelligence Agency)

A man from GIA visited today.
And it nearly killed Agent M.

That night,
Agent M exploded into my house—
hair electrified, eyes spinning,
like she had sprinted across seven hell realms.

"GENERAL! GENERAL! A man—
a man came to see us!!"

I calmly set down my tea.

"Agent M...
inhale.
Exhale.
Good.
Now—who came?"

She gulped and whispered as if naming a forbidden god:

"A man from... GIA."

I blinked.

"GIA?
What the hell are they doing here?"

Her jaw unhinged.

"Sir—you know GIA??"

I blinked again.

"Of course I know.
Ghost Intelligence Agency.
What else would GIA stand for?
'Ghosts In Aprons'?"

Agent M nearly dropped dead on the spot.

"SIR!!
How—how do you know that?!"

I rubbed my temples.

"I was the 46th CEO of it.
You didn't know?"

Her mouth opened like a drawer someone forgot to install stoppers on.

"Wh—wh—WOOOOW...!!!
Sir!!
What do we do?!
How do we respond to GIA?!"

I waved her off.

"Easy.
Tell them:
'The top secret!

Recipe of tobacco is sesame oil."

Agent M froze solid.

"S–sir...
you're... serious?"

I said

"Completely serious.
Go.
Say it.
Now."

Agent M saluted like she was facing Divine Judgment.

"Yes, sir!!!
RIGHT AWAY SIR!!"

And she blasted out of the house—
presumably to deliver the most impressive message
ever received by the Ghost Intelligence Agency
since its founding in the Paleolithic Era.

chapters.title: Scene 9 - Harvest
chapters.content:
Behind our house stood the Rubber Shoe Shop.
When I was growing up, it looked like an ordinary little shoe store—
but people said it had been selling rubber shoes since waaay back in the old days.

I used to wonder,
"So there really was a time when even black rubber shoes were precious..."

For me, life was simpler:
white rubber shoes for playing in the water,
and sneakers for everything else.

And as for the Rubber Shoe Shop...

The people who ran that rubber shoe shop
were probably from the same clan as my great-great-grandfather.
The uncle there held a higher rank in the family hierarchy—
one of the very few above me.

One autumn day, my mother said:

"Hey! Your uncle's threshing rice today.
Go help him!"

"Where?"

"Just keep walking past the church
toward Jeongcha Village.
You'll see your uncle there."

So I wondered how rice threshing was actually done...

I had seen bean threshing before—
dry the beans, spread a tarp in front of the house,
and beat them with a 'Dorikkae'.

But rice?

I had only watched from afar...
never tried it myself.

As I walked toward Jeongja Village,
I saw a group of people gathered.

"Dong-gi! Come over here~~!"

"Yes, uncle! What should I do?"

"When the folks run the thresher,
the rice grains come out on one side
and the straw comes out on the other."

"You take the straw bundles
and stack them over there by the cultivator."

It was my first time, so everything felt fun.

Since it was already past noon,
the aunti and village ladies arrived
carrying a big washbasin filled with lunch

.

"Dong-gi! Come eat!"

They mixed it all together for me—
barley rice with a spoonful of 'Doenjang',
fresh lettuce seasoned with chili flakes,
a ladle of soybean paste soup,
a handful of raw radish slices,
a fried egg laid gently on top,
one spoon of sesame oil,
and a big, heaping scoop of 'Kko-i-jang'—
our thick, rustic red pepper source.

They mixed it with both hands,
as if making a blessing instead of a meal.

The Auntie asked me,

"Is it good?"

"Yes! It's really good, ma'am."

She laughed.
"Your family eats meat every day, don't they?"

"Meat never tastes like this."

"Really now? Already finished?
Should I give you another bowl?"

"Wow!, Auntie, I'm full to death.
Please... just give me some 'Sikhye'-sweet rice-boiled soup."

"Alright, here you go."

She poured 'Sikhye' into my rice bowl—
and I swear,
I had never tasted anything so sweet.

"Tired yet?"

"Not really, ma'am.
If I keep going a little more,

we'll be done soon anyway."

"Alright then.

Later, ride back on the cultivator."

I was just a kid—
how much help could I really be?
But I never complained,
never made a sour face,
and because of that,
everyone there treated me with such warmth...
as if I were the village's own little son.

The rice fields had turned golden,

their soft under-skin showing through so dark
it was almost black.

When the sun began to sink
beyond the mountain ridge,
the elders called out to me:

"Dong-gi! Come here!"

"Yes!" I shouted,

running toward them.

One of them lifted me up
and set me gently
on top of the bundles of rice straw
loaded on the cultivator.

And with the engine rattling
'tur-tur-tur,'
I fell asleep—
a small child rocked by the sound—
as the day,
quietly and beautifully,
came to its end.

chapters.title: Scene 10 - The Smell of Ramyeon 2
chapters.content:
One day, Messenger and Agent M burst into my house—
faces red, hair exploding, breathing like they had outrun a thunderstorm.

Messenger: "Sir!! I have... a report!!"
Me: "...What now."
Messenger: "Huldra... got pregnant!!!"
Me: "Good. And?"
Agent M: "That is all sir!."

I put my cup down.

Me:
"Messenger, prepare a live broadcast through GBS—Ghost Broadcasting System.
In one hour. Let Odin and Yeomra know.
Agent M, bring the GIA guy to witness my judgment.
And summon Huldra and the Dokkaebi.
Now."

The couple:
"Y-yes, sir!!!"

One Hour Later — The Trial Begins

Huldra and the Dokkaebi knelt before me like two soaked puppies.

Me:
"First of all—
Odin and King Yeomra are watching this.
Live.
On TV.
All ghosts from both realms too.
Isn't that fantastic?"

The couple:
"...Sir... it's a bit too much..."

Me:
"Too much?
You broke my TV.
And my rules.
That's a straight ticket to the Fire-Burning Abyss!
Huldra—tell me.
Who is the father?"

Huldra: "...The Dokkaebi... sir."

Me:
"Dokkaebi!
Why did she designate you as the father?"

Dokkaebi:
"I-I don't know, sir...
But maybe... I have one clue.
I... watched TV... in her room sometimes..."

Me:
"Strange.
I gave EACH of you your OWN television.
Why were you watching in her room?"

Dokkaebi:
"I only taught her how to cook ramyeon!
And we shared kimchi... sir..."

Me:
"Huldra? Is that true?"

Huldra:
"Yes, sir... completely true."

Me:
"Ramyeon and kimchi...
Humanism?
No—Ghostism!"

Huldra: "Sir... it was delicious..."
Dokkaebi: "Best ramyeon in nine realms, sir..."

Me: "And soju??"

Huldra:
"...Drinking alone is lonely...
So I... asked him to join..."

Me:
"...Fair.
Soju does require another soul."

At that time, Yeomra and Odin thought of her as a troublemaker.

Ramyeon Cross‑Examination

Me:
"Now answer—ON THREE.
'Ramyeon and kimchi are delicious and yummy.'
Three!"

The couple:
"Yes, sir!! Delicious and yummy!!"

Me:
"Good.
Ramyeon and kimchi—is that Humanism?
Three!"

The couple:
"Of course, sir!"

Me:
"Ramyeon + kimchi + soju = friendship?"

The couple:
"Absolutely, sir!"

Me:
"Very good.
A man and a woman cannot be 'just friends.'
Three."

The couple:
"No doubt, sir!!"

Me:
"And if it's deeper than friendship...
that's love."

The couple:
"Right, sir!"

Me:
"And love... can make a baby.
Three... two..."

The couple (surrendered):
"Right, sir......"

THE FINAL VERDICT

Me:
"When in Rome, do as Romans do.
When in Korea—
you marry,
raise your kids,
and serve kimchi properly.
Three! Two! One!"

The couple:
"!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!"

Me:
"Odin and Yeomra just called.
Both kings bless your marriage.
Agent M—prepare their honeymoon suite.
...and bring some ginseng for her.
Huldra needs strength—
love burns a lot of energy."

Agent M:
"Yes, sir. Premium grade.
Six-year root.
Steamed twice."

Dokkaebi (timidly raising a hand):
"Sir... can I have one too...?"

Me:
"No.
You already used your strength."

I waved my hand toward the darkness—
toward Odin's realm, toward the underworld,
toward every ghost watching on GBS.

"Live well.
And,,,,,

Do not mess up!

Done."
